doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Listening habits: New York Dixieland versus traditional jazz
summary: They listened to the New York scene, not Turk Murphy or Kid Ory, which Mead now explores.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: But just to finish up one thing, so we didn’t think of ourselves in the Catatonic Five as playing traditional jazz. And we frankly didn’t listen to a lot of traditional jazz. I mean we were much more listening to the stuff that was going on in New York, so Turk Murphy and Kid Ory and stuff like that, not that we didn’t like it we just didn’t deal with that very much.

Right. I think it’s how musicians usually learn music is they grab what’s happening at the time and then if they get interested to go backwards they will. Like gee where did this come from, who do you suppose these people listened to.
That’s exactly what’s happened to me. I mean now at the age of 69 I’m actually going back and listening to Kid Ory and George Brunies and some of these people and it’s remarkable stuff.
